name: Hereditary Spastic Paraplegia

ethnicAssociations: SPG11 more common in Mediterranean and Middle Eastern populations
Prevalence varies by population due to founder mutations

criteria.description: Progressive spastic gait with bilateral lower limb spasticity and weakness
Lower limb hyperreflexia with extensor plantar responses
Family history consistent with known inheritance pattern (AD, AR, or X-linked)
Pathogenic mutation in a known HSP gene
Exclusion of structural, metabolic, and acquired causes of spastic paraplegia

diagnosticCriteria.minimumForDiagnosis: Progressive bilateral lower limb spasticity and weakness with exclusion of alternative causes. Family history or genetic confirmation strongly supports diagnosis. Classified as pure (uncomplicated) or complicated based on additional features.
diagnosticCriteria.notes: Over 80 SPG loci identified. Most common: SPG4 (spastin, AD, ~40% of AD-HSP), SPG3A (atlastin, AD, childhood onset), SPG7 (paraplegin, AR), SPG11 (spatacsin, AR, complicated with thin corpus callosum). Pure vs complicated classification guides genetic testing.

pathognomonic.notes: Bilateral, symmetric; scissoring gait; the defining feature
searchTerms: slowly developing walking difficulty with stiffness
spasticity and hyperreflexia in lower limbs
tight muscles and overactive reflexes in legs

pathognomonic.notes: Typically progresses over years to decades
searchTerms: symptoms start slowly and worsen over time

common.symptomName: Lower limb weakness (mainly hip flexors and tibialis anterior)
searchTerms: weakness mainly in hip and shin muscles
lower limb weakness affecting hip flexors and tibialis anterior
muscle weakness in front thigh and shin

common.symptomName: Impaired vibration sense in lower limbs
common.notes: Dorsal column involvement in pure HSP
searchTerms: impaired vibration sense in lower limbs
reduced ability to sense vibrations in feet
abnormal foot shape with high arch

common.symptomName: Low back pain and leg pain
common.notes: From chronic spasticity and altered gait mechanics
searchTerms: pain in lower back and legs

occasional.notes: SPG11, SPG15; associated with cognitive decline

rare.notes: Dystonia or parkinsonism in rare subtypes

laboratory: Very long chain fatty acids to exclude adrenomyeloneuropathy
Vitamin B12 and copper levels to exclude metabolic myelopathy
imaging: MRI spine: usually normal or may show spinal cord atrophy in long-standing cases
MRI brain: thin corpus callosum (SPG11, SPG15), white matter abnormalities (complicated forms)
Normal MRI spine needed to exclude structural causes
genetic: SPG4 (SPAST/spastin): most common AD form (~40% of AD-HSP); pure HSP
SPG3A (ATL1/atlastin): second most common AD form; early childhood onset
SPG7 (SPG7/paraplegin): common AR form; cerebellar ataxia and optic atrophy
SPG11 (SPG11/spatacsin): most common AR form; complicated with thin corpus callosum
Gene panel or whole exome sequencing recommended for diagnosis
Over 80 SPG loci and >60 identified genes
other: Nerve conduction studies and EMG: may show subclinical neuropathy in some forms
Visual evoked potentials: may be abnormal

distinguishingFeatures: MS has dissemination in space and time on MRI
MS has oligoclonal bands in CSF
MS has brain white matter lesions
ALS has combined UMN and LMN signs with progressive weakness
ALS has muscle atrophy and fasciculations
ALS has rapid progression (years not decades)
ALS has EMG showing active denervation
FA has prominent ataxia as primary feature
FA has areflexia (not hyperreflexia) due to neuropathy
FA has GAA repeat expansion in FXN gene

redFlags: Rapidly progressive spasticity should prompt consideration of acquired causes (MS, ALS, structural lesion)
Adrenomyeloneuropathy must be excluded in males with progressive spastic paraplegia (VLCFA testing)
Dopa-responsive dystonia can mimic HSP in children and responds dramatically to levodopa
Absence of family history does not exclude HSP (de novo mutations, AR inheritance, incomplete penetrance)
Complicated features (cognitive decline, neuropathy, ataxia) guide genetic subtyping
Vitamin B12 and copper deficiency are treatable mimics that must be excluded
references: Shribman S, et al. Hereditary spastic paraplegia: from diagnosis to emerging therapeutic approaches. Lancet Neurol. 2019;18(12):1136-1146.
Fink JK. Hereditary spastic paraplegia: clinico-pathologic features and emerging molecular mechanisms. Acta Neuropathol. 2013;126(3):307-328.
Blackstone C. Hereditary spastic paraplegia. Handb Clin Neurol. 2018;148:633-652.
